Do People Get More Conservative With Age?

records.content:
There’s a famous (but unattributable) quip that goes something like this:

If you are not a liberal at 25, you have no heart. If you are not a conservative at 35, you have no brain.

In Chapter 12 of 

Probably Overthinking It, I used data from the General Social Survey (GSS) to show that the quip is half right. Older people are more likely to say they are conservative, and they hold more conservative views.

But as people get older, their views don’t become more conservative; on average, they become a little more liberal. I called this combination 

the Overton paradox.

That analysis used data through 2021 and methods that were good enough for the chapter. Since then, the GSS has released data from 2022 and 2024, and while working on my next book, 

You Would Choose Now, I developed better methods for separating the effects of age, birth year, and current events. So it’s time for an update.

This is the first in a series of articles. In this one, we’ll see whether people get more conservative as they get older. The answer is still no.

Do People Get More Conservative With Age?

records.content:
If someone says people get more conservative with age, what do they mean? I assume that people have in mind some bundle of beliefs, attitudes, and behaviors they consider conservative. But different people might imagine a different bundle.

For the book, I searched the GSS for the questions that most distinguish liberals and conservatives, and then I curated a list of 15 that cover a variety of topics and were asked often over the course of the survey. That worked well enough, but curating involves judgment calls, which is where researcher bias can sneak in.

This time I replaced curation with a mostly automated selection process that starts with 6,943 variables in the GSS dataset and selects 53 questions that meet the requirements (described at the end of this article).

To combine responses to 53 questions into a single measure, I use a Bayesian IRT (item response theory) model to estimate a latent factor of conservatism for each of 64,632 respondents from 1972 to 2024 who were asked and answered at least five questions.
This model makes it possible to compare people who answered different sets of questions, even in cases where there is no overlap.
More details about the process are in 

this technical appendix.

Finally, for each respondent, we express their estimated conservatism as a percentage, which you can think of as the number of conservative responses they would give to a hypothetical pool of 100 questions.

Now let’s see some results.

records.content:
If you think about the people you know, it’s likely that the older ones are more conservative, on average, than the younger ones.

To see what that difference looks like in the data, I divided the respondents by the decade when they were interviewed and computed the average percentage of conservative responses as a function of age.

The following figure shows the results, with one line for each decade of the survey from the 1970s to the 2020s.



Figure 1:Percent conservative responses by age, for each decade of surveys.

We can see two trends:

In every decade, older people give more conservative answers than younger people. In the 1970s, conservatism increased by about 3.9 percentage points per decade of age. Since then the slope has been a little smaller, about 2.9 points per decade in the 1980s and 1990s, and 2.1 to 2.4 points per decade since 2000. But in every decade, the oldest respondents are 15 to 25 points more conservative than the youngest.

The figure also shows that every line is lower than the one before. At every age, people surveyed in the 2020s are more liberal than people the same age surveyed in the 1970s. Keep that in mind; it will be important.

So the first half of the quip is right: older people are more conservative.
But that doesn’t mean that people become more conservative as they get older.

records.content:
To see why, let’s group people by decade of birth. The following figure shows percent conservative responses as a function of age again, but this time each line represents a decade of birth, from the 1900s to the 2000s.



Figure 2:Percent conservative responses by age, for each decade of birth: the updated version of the figure in the book.

Within each group, the lines are mostly flat or declining. As people get older, they don’t become more conservative.

If this seems like a contradiction, remember Simpson’s paradox, which I wrote about in 

this previous post and in 

Chapter 11 of Probably Overthinking It: the trend in every group goes one way, and the overall trend goes the other way.

However, this figure has a subtle problem. Each line represents people born over a ten-year span, and the mix of birth years changes as we follow the line. At the beginning of each line, it includes only the oldest members of the cohort, and at the end it includes only the youngest.

I was aware of this problem when I was working on Probably Overthinking It. Now I have a way to solve it.

records.content:
The solution is to estimate a trajectory for each birth year and then aggregate the results, rather than aggregating before estimating.
But with less data for each birth year, we need a model to smooth out the estimates.

I developed a model that solves this problem, which I described in 

this blog post.
This model is also the kernel of the analysis I’m doing for my new book-in-progress, 

You Would Choose Now.

The model estimates a component for each year of birth and a component for each year of the survey. Together, they describe a trajectory for each birth year over the years it was observed. The following figure shows those trajectories.



Figure 3:Estimated percent conservative responses for each birth year, from the period–cohort model.

Each line represents a single birth year. For example, the yellow-green line at the top left shows people born in 1900, who were 72 when the survey started in 1972. The purple line at the bottom right shows people born in 2006, who became eligible for the survey when they turned 18 in 2024.

Two patterns are clear:

Each birth year starts out more liberal than the one before. People born in 1900 gave conservative answers to about two-thirds of the questions; people born after 2000 give conservative answers to about 40%.

As each birth year ages, its line drifts down. Following the same people over time, their answers become more liberal, not more conservative.

We can decompose these results into a cohort component that shows how conservatism varies from one birth year to the next, controlling for changes over time, and a period component that shows how conservatism varies from year to year, controlling for generational replacement.

The following figure shows the cohort component: the average level of conservatism for each birth year, as if every birth year had been surveyed in every year of the survey.



Figure 4:Cohort component: where each birth year starts.

The decline is steepest between people born in the 1930s and 1950s; it pauses for people born in the 1950s and 1960s, and it continues after that.

The following figure shows the period component: the average level of conservatism in each year of the survey, as if the population had the same mix of birth years throughout.



Figure 5:Period component: how everyone moves together.

With the mix of birth years held constant, conservatism declines slowly. From 1972 to 2024, the total change within cohorts is −4.6 percentage points. If we fit a straight line, the rate of change is −0.82 percentage points per decade, with a 90% interval from −0.97 to −0.66. So the change is small, but we can be confident about the direction: following the same people over time, they become a little more liberal.

Finally, we can use these components to break down the total change. Over the course of the survey, average conservatism fell by 16.4 percentage points. Of that, about 11.8 points are due to generational replacement — older, more conservative people leaving the survey population and younger, more liberal people joining it — and about 4.6 points are due to changing minds. So more than two-thirds of the change is generational.

The model in the previous section is based on the simplifying assumption that the cohort and period components don’t interact. In reality, they might; for example, if an event affects one cohort more than another.

To see whether this assumption is a reasonable modeling decision, we can fit the same model separately for each decade of birth, and see what the trend looks like in each group.

The following figure shows the period component for each decade of birth, holding its mix of birth years fixed, so the shifting composition of each group can’t move the line.



Figure 6:Conservatism within cohorts, for each decade of birth.

Within the groups, the lines are flat or declining. People born in the 1950s moved a little toward conservative until about 1980, and toward liberal after that.

The dotted line shows the overall average, which falls faster than most of the groups, because it includes the effect of generational replacement.

The following figure shows the same analysis with respondents grouped by social generation, using the Pew Research Center’s definitions.



Figure 7:Conservatism within cohorts, for each generation. The dotted line is the overall average.

The results are the same: no group of birth years, defined either way, became more conservative over the course of the survey. All of them became more liberal or stayed about the same.

All of these results depend on the set of questions I chose.
So if you think I chose badly, you might not be convinced by my conclusion.

For example, you might think the questions I selected put too much weight on social issues and not enough on economic issues. You might not agree with my decision to exclude religious beliefs or confidence in institutions. Or you might think there should be more questions about crime.

In future articles, I’ll run the analysis with different bundles of variables. We’ll see that the results are quite robust — pretty much any bundle of questions that covers a mixture of topics leads to the same conclusions: people do not become more conservative with age.

But if you don’t want to wait, you can try it yourself. I have created an online calculator, called 

The Overtron, where you can select whatever bundle of questions you want and run the whole analysis in your browser.
Try it out, and let me know what you find!

records.content:
Here are the details of the selection process I used. In general, I tried to keep my judgment out of it, but you’ll see that there are a couple of steps where I intervened.

Start with everything. The GSS cumulative file has 6,943 variables. I kept the ones that record responses to questions asked in at least 8 waves over a span of at least 15 years, with between 2 and 7 possible answers. That leaves 429.

Keep the opinions. From those, I kept the questions that ask for an opinion about a public issue or a social norm. I left out demographics (like age and income), behavior (like smoking or owning a gun), personal circumstances (like happiness and health), and, as I did for the book, religious belief and practice (we’ll revisit that one). I also left out questions about party and voting, which would make the measure circular. That eliminates 259 and leaves 170 questions.

Identify the conservative answers. For each question, I split the answers into two groups at the point that best separates people who identify as conservative from people who identify as liberal. The answers conservatives choose more often are the conservative side. For example, if the question is “Do you favor or oppose the death penalty for persons convicted of murder?”, the conservative answer is “Favor”.

Measure how well each question separates them. For each question, I estimated how strongly the conservative answer is associated with self-identified ideology, controlling for the year of the survey and the respondent’s year of birth. Steps 3 and 4 don’t eliminate any questions.

Coverage. For the final list, a question had to be asked in at least half of the survey years (16 of 32). That’s because the measure compares people surveyed decades apart, so we need long-running questions that overlap in time. If too many questions are short-lived, people surveyed in different years would be measured by different questions, and changes over time would mix real changes in beliefs with changes in the questions. This step eliminates 49 questions and leaves 121.

Stability. The difference between conservatives and liberals couldn’t reverse. If the same answer was given more often by conservatives in one decade and by liberals in another, the question is not a stable indicator of conservatism. This step eliminates 1 question and leaves 120.

No duplicates. Some questions were asked with two different wordings, on different versions of the survey, so I kept one of each pair. And when several questions cover the same topic, I kept the one that best separates conservatives and liberals, from step 4. This step eliminates 53 questions (12 alternate wordings and 41 others on the same topic) and leaves 67.

No confidence questions. I left out 13 questions about confidence in institutions — like the press, organized religion, and the military — because they evaluate institutions rather than take a position on an issue. I made this decision after seeing results that included them, so in a later article I’ll show what difference they make. One of the 13 was already eliminated in step 6, so this step eliminates 12 and leaves 55.

Check for drift. A question “drifts” if its connection to conservatism changes over time. This step ended up excluding only two questions, so it doesn’t have much impact on the results. The details are in the 

technical appendix. That leaves the 53 questions I used.

records.content:
The period–cohort model in this project fits two second-order random walks (RW2): one over birth years and one over survey years. Fitted with NUTS in its usual form, almost every draw needs about 1,000 leapfrog steps. This memo describes a change of variables that leaves the model unchanged but cuts the time per fit by 6–20×:

write the RW2 prior in the eigenbasis of its covariance matrix;

split the walk’s linear trend out as a separate coordinate.

The prior, the likelihood, and the posterior over everything the model reports stay the same. Only the coordinates the sampler moves in change.

The code is rw2(..., form="trend") in overton/apc.py. The check that both forms are the same model is overton/rw2_trend.py, and the experiments are in docs/lab.md.

records.content:
The model is CultureWar’s model10 as ported to overton/apc.py. Each cohort × year cell has a weighted mean score \bar y_{ct}, observed with standard error \sigma^{\text{resid}}_t / \sqrt{n^{\text{eff}}_{ct}}, around\operatorname{logit}^{-1}\left(\alpha + f^{\text{cohort}}_c + f^{\text{period}}_t + \epsilon_t\right),

where \epsilon is zero-sum year noise. With the p48 question set, there are 2,442 cells, 124 birth years, 53 survey years, and 284 free parameters.

Each walk f of length n is a mean-centered RW2, built by double cumulative sums with a free initial slope:z \sim \mathcal N(0, I_{n-2}), \qquad v_0 \sim \mathcal N(0, 0.2^2), \qquad
f = \sigma\, P L z + v_0\, r .

L is the n \times (n-2) double-cumsum map from innovations to levels, with f_{\text{raw},0} = 0 and the first slope 0. Row k of L is (k-1, k-2, \ldots, 1, 0, \ldots, 0).

P = I - \tfrac1n \mathbf 1 \mathbf 1^\top removes the mean.

r = P\,(0, 1, \ldots, n-1)^\top is the mean-centered ramp, which the initial slope v_0 scales.

\sigma is the walk’s scale. It has an exponential prior.

This is the standard non-centered form. The sampler moves in (z, v_0, \log\sigma).

records.content:
NUTS with a diagonal mass matrix can rescale each coordinate, but it can’t rotate them. When the posterior is strongly correlated in the sampler’s coordinates, trajectories need many small steps.

On the saved draws of the decided p48 fit, the posterior’s correlation matrix in the sampler’s coordinates has a condition number of about 9,200. Its smallest-variance directions are smooth shapes of the cohort curve over the data-rich birth years:

Many coordinates per shape. The data pin down each smooth shape well. But in innovation coordinates, a smooth shape is a weighted sum of about 50 entries of z, so the posterior is narrow along a direction that no single coordinate represents.

A funnel. The walk is \sigma times the innovations, so each well-identified shape also couples z to \sigma.

The ramp twice over. The smoothest of these shapes is nearly the linear ramp r, which v_0 also scales. So v_0 and the smoothest innovations trade off against each other.

As a result, the production fit (nutpie, 4 chains × (4000 + 6000), target_accept 0.99) reached the maximum tree depth of 10 on every draw. That’s 1,023 gradient evaluations per draw.

records.content:
Given \sigma, the walk without the slope term, \sigma P L z, is Gaussian with covariance \sigma^2 P L L^\top P. Take its eigendecomposition and keep the n-2 nonzero eigenvalues:P L L^\top P = U \Lambda U^\top, \qquad M = U \Lambda^{1/2} \quad (n \times (n-2)).

Now definew = Q z, \qquad Q = M^{+} P L ,

where M^{+} is the pseudoinverse. Since M has full column rank and (PL)(PL)^\top = M M^\top, Q is square and orthogonal, and PLz = Mw. So:

w \sim \mathcal N(0, I), exactly as z is;

the change of variables has Jacobian 1;

f = \sigma M w + v_0 r is the same walk.

Each column of M is one shape of the walk, from smoothest (largest \lambda) to roughest. A smooth shape the data pin down is now a single coordinate w_k, and the mass matrix can scale it.

On its own, this roughly doubled the ESS per minute (with TyMC and PyMC-style adaptation). But with nutpie-style adaptation, a few coordinates mixed badly (ESS 10–20). Those were the smoothest shapes and v_0.

records.content:
The smoothest columns of M are close to the ramp r, so v_0 and the leading w_k explain nearly the same thing: the walk’s overall linear trend. The fix is to make that trend a coordinate of its own. Decompose M into its projection on r and the rest:a = \frac{M^\top r}{r^\top r}, \qquad M_\perp = \left(I - \frac{r r^\top}{r^\top r}\right) M, \qquad M = r a^\top + M_\perp .

Thenf = \sigma M_\perp w + \beta\, r, \qquad \beta = v_0 + \sigma\, a^\top w .

\beta is the walk’s total linear trend, and M_\perp w has no linear component. The map (v_0, w) \mapsto (\beta, w) is a shear with Jacobian 1. So the same model is:

w \sim \mathcal N(0, I);

\beta with a flat prior;

v_0’s prior, \mathcal N(0, 0.2^2), added as a potential evaluated at v_0 = \beta - \sigma a^\top w.

The data identify \beta directly, as the trend of the curve, and in these coordinates it no longer competes with the smooth shapes.

records.content:
The basis is computed once in numpy. In PyMC (overton/apc.py):def rw2_trend_basis(n):
    L = np.zeros((n, n - 2))
    for k in range(2, n):
        L[k, : k - 1] = np.arange(k - 1, 0, -1)
    P = np.eye(n) - 1 / n
    lam, U = np.linalg.eigh(P @ L @ L.T @ P)
    keep = lam > 1e-9 * lam.max()
    M = U[:, keep] * np.sqrt(lam[keep])
    r = P @ np.arange(n, dtype=float)
    a = M.T @ r / (r @ r)
    return M - np.outer(r, a), r, a


# inside rw2(name, n, sigma, slope_init_scale, dims, form="trend")
M_perp, r, a = rw2_trend_basis(n)
w = pm.Normal(f"{name}_w", 0.0, 1.0, shape=n - 2)
beta = pm.Flat(f"{name}_trend")
v0 = beta - sigma * pm.math.dot(a, w)
pm.Potential(f"{name}_slope_init_prior", pm.logp(pm.Normal.dist(0.0, slope_init_scale), v0))
f = pm.Deterministic(name, sigma * pm.math.dot(M_perp, w) + beta * r, dims=dims)

The TyMC version, used by the browser page, is rw2_trend in overtron/spike/model.ts.

Centering. Sampling the levels of the walk directly made the conditioning worse by 35–175×, as screened on the saved draws (not sampled). Neighboring levels of a smooth curve are nearly collinear. In CultureWar’s period-only time model on binomial series, centering did help, so the answer depends on the model and the data.

Moving the slope’s anchor. Making the free slope the one at a middle birth year, instead of the first, didn’t change the conditioning.

Threads. The trend form multiplies by a dense n \times (n-2) matrix in every gradient. With default settings, BLAS may start its own threads in every chain. But the product is only about 15,000 multiply-adds, too small to be worth splitting across threads. Set OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1.

Laptop (12 cores): p48 period–cohort fit, 4 × (1000 + 1000). One thread per chain took 25 s on about 3 cores. The default took 56 s with 70 threads on about 10 cores.

Unity (AMD EPYC 7402): the same fit at production length, after a warm-up, each configuration twice. With 4 or 16 cores and one or default threads, every run took 109–115 s.

So the setting helps on one machine and costs nothing on the other. Extra cores don’t speed up a single fit either: put them into more chains or more fits.

Prior predictive. pm.Flat and pm.Potential can’t be forward-sampled. Draw prior predictive samples from the current form, which is the same model.

Scope. The derivation covers the Gaussian RW2 with a free initial slope. A Student-t RW2 isn’t Gaussian, so the eigenbasis argument doesn’t apply. A walk without the free slope has no v_0 to absorb a^\top w, so it would need its own derivation.

Default since 2026-11-03. New fits use the trend form, and --rw2-form cumsum selects the current form. Results fitted before then used the current form. Summaries record which form was used.

The data come from the 

General Social Survey (GSS) cumulative file, 1972 to 2024, release 3a. The excerpt contains one row per respondent and one column for each of the 170 candidate questions described below, plus year, age, year of birth, self-identified ideology (polviews), and the analysis weight.

The sample excludes 2021, and in 2022 and 2024 it includes only respondents interviewed in person or by phone. In those years the GSS also used a web questionnaire, and the answers people give on the web differ systematically from the ones they give to an interviewer. records.content:
For each question and decade, the gap is the weighted percentage of conservatives who gave the conservative answer, minus the percentage of liberals, with a 90% interval based on Kish’s effective sample size. Decades with fewer than 200 liberal and conservative respondents are left out.

A question is excluded if the gap reverses: in one decade, conservatives are credibly more likely to give the conservative answer, by at least 5 percentage points, and in another decade liberals are credibly more likely, by at least 5 points. (“Credibly” means the 90% interval excludes 0.)

A gap that shrinks is allowed. When nearly everyone gives the same answer, the gap between any two groups has to shrink, even if the question means the same thing.

REVERSAL_POINTS = 5
MIN_RESPONDENTS = 200
Z90 = norm.ppf(0.95)


def weighted_share(y, w):
    """Weighted mean and its standard error, using Kish's effective sample size."""
    p = np.average(y, weights=w)
    n_eff = w.sum() ** 2 / (w**2).sum()
    return p, np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n_eff)


def decade_gaps(v):
    df = pd.DataFrame(dict(y=coded[v], p=gss["polviews3"], w=gss["weight"], decade=gss["decade"])).dropna()
    df = df[df["p"].isin(["Liberal", "Conservative"])]
    rows = []
    for d, group in df.groupby("decade"):
        con, lib = group[group["p"] == "Conservative"], group[group["p"] == "Liberal"]
        if len(group) < MIN_RESPONDENTS or len(con) == 0 or len(lib) == 0:
            continue
        pc, sc = weighted_share(con["y"].values, con["w"].values)
        pl, sl = weighted_share(lib["y"].values, lib["w"].values)
        gap, se = (pc - pl) * 100, np.hypot(sc, sl) * 100
        rows.append(dict(decade=d, gap=gap, lo=gap - Z90 * se, hi=gap + Z90 * se))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


def reverses(gaps):
    con_ahead = (gaps["lo"] > 0) & (gaps["gap"] >= REVERSAL_POINTS)
    lib_ahead = (gaps["hi"] < 0) & (gaps["gap"] <= -REVERSAL_POINTS)
    return bool(con_ahead.any() and lib_ahead.any())

records.content:
Respondents in different years answered different subsets of the questions: questions were added and dropped over the decades, and the GSS asks many of them on only some versions of the survey. So a simple count of conservative answers isn’t comparable from one respondent to another. Instead, I use a one-parameter item response (Rasch) model:

each respondent has a latent conservatism, \theta;

each question has a difficulty, d;

the probability of a conservative answer is \mathrm{expit}(\theta - d).

A question with a high difficulty is one that only the most conservative respondents answer conservatively.

The latent conservatism is represented on a grid of 21 values from −6 to 6, with a wide normal prior (standard deviation 4).

XS = np.linspace(-6, 6, 21)
PRIOR = norm.pdf(XS, 0, 4)
PRIOR /= PRIOR.sum()
MIN_ANSWERED = 5


def log_likelihoods(a, d, xs=XS):
    """Each question's log likelihood on the grid: shape (questions, respondents, grid).

    a: array of 1/0/NaN answers (respondents x questions); d: difficulties
    """
    P = expit(xs[None, :] - d[:, None])
    out = np.zeros((a.shape[1], a.shape[0], len(xs)))
    for j in range(a.shape[1]):
        col = a[:, j, None]
        out[j] = np.where(col == 1, np.log(P[j]), np.where(col == 0, np.log(1 - P[j]), 0))
    return out


def grid_posterior(a, d, prior=PRIOR, xs=XS):
    """Each respondent's posterior on the grid."""
    loglike = log_likelihoods(a, d, xs).sum(axis=0)
    posterior = np.exp(loglike - loglike.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)) * prior
    return posterior / posterior.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)

records.content:
The difficulties are estimated once, from all years combined, by weighted marginal maximum likelihood, using the EM algorithm of Bock and Aitkin:

E step: each respondent’s posterior on the grid, given the current difficulties;

M step: for each question, the difficulty at which the weighted expected share of conservative answers, among the respondents who were asked, equals the observed weighted share.

The calibration uses respondents who answered at least 5 of the questions. It stops when no difficulty changes by more than 0.0001, or after 100 iterations.

def em_difficulties(coded, weights, tol=1e-4, max_iter=100):
    a = coded.values
    w = np.asarray(weights, dtype=float)
    asked = ~np.isnan(a)
    share = np.nansum(a * w[:, None], axis=0) / (asked * w[:, None]).sum(axis=0)
    d = -np.log(share / (1 - share))  # start: minus the logit of the prevalence
    for _ in range(max_iter):
        posterior = grid_posterior(a, d)
        new = d.copy()
        for j in range(a.shape[1]):
            mass = (w[asked[:, j], None] * posterior[asked[:, j]]).sum(axis=0)
            target = (w[asked[:, j]] * a[asked[:, j], j]).sum()
            new[j] = brentq(lambda dj: (mass * expit(XS - dj)).sum() - target, -10, 10)
        change = np.abs(new - d).max()
        d = new
        if change < tol:
            break
    return pd.Series(d, coded.columns)


def calibrate(names):
    """EM difficulties for a set of questions, from respondents who answered at least MIN_ANSWERED."""
    sub = coded[names]
    keep = (sub.notna().sum(axis=1) >= MIN_ANSWERED).values
    return em_difficulties(sub[keep], gss.loc[keep, "weight"])

DRIFT_THRESHOLD = 0.5  # logits


def drift(names, only=None):
    """Decade effects for each question, controlling for its leave-one-out score."""
    d = calibrate(names)
    a = coded[names].values
    ll = log_likelihoods(a, d.values)
    total = ll.sum(axis=0)
    answered = ~np.isnan(a)
    n_answered = answered.sum(axis=1)
    rows = []
    for j, v in enumerate(names):
        if only and v not in only:
            continue
        keep = answered[:, j] & (n_answered - 1 >= MIN_ANSWERED)
        loo = total[keep] - ll[j, keep]
        post = np.exp(loo - loo.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)) * PRIOR
        score = (post / post.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)) @ XS
        y, w, decade = a[keep, j], gss["weight"].values[keep], gss["decade"].values[keep]
        counts = pd.Series(decade).value_counts()
        ok = np.isin(decade, counts.index[counts >= MIN_RESPONDENTS])
        decades = np.sort(np.unique(decade[ok]))
        X = np.column_stack([score[ok]] + [(decade[ok] == k).astype(float) for k in decades])
        res = sm.GLM(y[ok], X, family=sm.families.Binomial(), var_weights=w[ok] / w[ok].mean()).fit(cov_type="HC1")
        k = len(decades)
        C = np.zeros((k, k + 1))
        C[:, 1:] = np.eye(k) - 1 / k  # each decade relative to the mean of the decades
        effect = C @ res.params
        se = np.sqrt(np.diag(C @ res.cov_params() @ C.T))
        listed = ((np.abs(effect) - Z90 * se > 0) & (np.abs(effect) >= DRIFT_THRESHOLD)).any()
        rows.append(dict(variable=v, description=meta.loc[v, "description"], slope=res.params[0], listed=listed,
                         **{f"{dec}s": e for dec, e in zip(decades, effect)}))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("variable")

records.content:
The trends over time, age, and year of birth are smooth curves with a second-order random walk (RW2) prior: each step’s change in slope is normal with standard deviation \sigma, and the curve is centered at 0 so it doesn’t compete with the intercept. Sampling the RW2 directly (as a double cumulative sum of innovations) is slow, because the innovations are strongly correlated in the posterior. The same prior can be written in other coordinates: the eigenvectors of the centered RW2 covariance, with the linear trend split out as a separate parameter. The two forms define the same model; the second samples several times faster. The derivation is in 

a separate note.

import pymc as pm


def rw2_trend_basis(n):
    """Eigenbasis of the centered RW2 prior, with the linear ramp split out."""
    L = np.zeros((n, n - 2))
    for k in range(2, n):
        L[k, : k - 1] = np.arange(k - 1, 0, -1)
    P = np.eye(n) - 1 / n
    lam, U = np.linalg.eigh(P @ L @ L.T @ P)
    keep = lam > 1e-9 * lam.max()
    M = U[:, keep] * np.sqrt(lam[keep])
    r = P @ np.arange(n, dtype=float)
    a = M.T @ r / (r @ r)
    return M - np.outer(r, a), r, a


def rw2(name, n, sigma, slope_init_scale, dims):
    """Centered RW2 with a free initial slope, in the trend form."""
    M_perp, r, a = rw2_trend_basis(n)
    w = pm.Normal(f"{name}_w", 0.0, 1.0, shape=n - 2)
    beta = pm.Flat(f"{name}_trend")
    v0 = beta - sigma * pm.math.dot(a, w)
    pm.Potential(f"{name}_slope_init_prior", pm.logp(pm.Normal.dist(0.0, slope_init_scale), v0))
    return pm.Deterministic(name, sigma * pm.math.dot(M_perp, w) + beta * r, dims=dims)

records.content:
Period (and age): a smooth curve over survey years (or ages), plus independent noise for each year, on the logit scale, fit to the cell means. This model is used for each group of self-identified ideology, and for each decade of birth.

Period–cohort: a smooth curve over years of birth (the cohort component) plus a smooth curve over survey years (the period component), plus year noise, fit to the cells of year of birth × survey year. The period component is the change within cohorts: how the beliefs of people born in the same year change over time. Following a birth cohort, age and period move together, so this change combines the effects of aging and of the times; the model doesn’t try to separate them.

The prior scales are the same as in You Would Choose Now.

PERIOD_SETTINGS = dict(sigma_t_scale=0.125, slope_init_scale=0.2, sigma_short_scale=0.5)
COHORT_SETTINGS = dict(sigma_c_scale=0.125, sigma_t_scale=0.125, slope_init_scale=0.2, sigma_short_scale=0.2,
                       sigma_resid_scale=0.5)


def series_model(cells, index, grid, s=PERIOD_SETTINGS):
    idx = cells[index].map({v: i for i, v in enumerate(grid)}).values
    se = np.sqrt(np.maximum(cells["var_weighted"].values, 1e-4) / np.maximum(cells["n_eff"].values, 1.0))
    with pm.Model(coords={"grid": grid}) as m:
        alpha = pm.Normal("alpha", 0.0, 1.0)
        sigma_t = pm.Exponential("sigma_t", 1.0 / s["sigma_t_scale"])
        trend = rw2("trend", len(grid), sigma_t, s["slope_init_scale"], dims="grid")
        eta = pm.Deterministic("eta", alpha + trend, dims="grid")
        pm.Deterministic("mu", pm.math.sigmoid(eta), dims="grid")
        sigma_short = pm.HalfNormal("sigma_short", s["sigma_short_scale"])
        epsilon_z = pm.ZeroSumNormal("epsilon_z", sigma=1.0, dims="grid")
        epsilon = pm.Deterministic("epsilon", sigma_short * epsilon_z, dims="grid")
        pm.Normal("y_mean", mu=pm.math.sigmoid(eta[idx] + epsilon[idx]), sigma=se, observed=cells["p_weighted"].values)
    return m


def period_cohort_model(cells, years, cohorts, s=COHORT_SETTINGS):
    t = cells["year"].map({v: i for i, v in enumerate(years)}).values
    c = cells["cohort"].map({v: i for i, v in enumerate(cohorts)}).values
    with pm.Model(coords={"year": years, "cohort_grid": cohorts}) as m:
        alpha = pm.Normal("alpha", 0.0, 1.0)
        sigma_c = pm.Exponential("sigma_c", 1.0 / s["sigma_c_scale"])
        cohort = rw2("cohort", len(cohorts), sigma_c, s["slope_init_scale"], dims="cohort_grid")
        sigma_t = pm.Exponential("sigma_t", 1.0 / s["sigma_t_scale"])
        period = rw2("period", len(years), sigma_t, s["slope_init_scale"], dims="year")
        sigma_short = pm.Exponential("sigma_short", 1.0 / s["sigma_short_scale"])
        epsilon_z = pm.ZeroSumNormal("epsilon_z", sigma=1.0, dims="year")
        epsilon = pm.Deterministic("epsilon", sigma_short * epsilon_z, dims="year")
        p_obs = pm.math.sigmoid(alpha + cohort[c] + period[t] + epsilon[t])
        sigma_resid = pm.HalfNormal("sigma_resid", s["sigma_resid_scale"], dims="year")
        pm.Normal("y_mean", mu=p_obs, sigma=sigma_resid[t] / np.sqrt(cells["n_eff"].values),
                  observed=cells["p_weighted"].values)
    return m

The production fits used 4 chains with 4,000 tuning steps and 6,000 draws each. To keep this notebook quick, it uses 2 chains with 1,000 tuning steps and 1,000 draws, and then compares the results with the production fits. It uses the nutpie sampler if it’s installed, and PyMC’s default sampler otherwise.

try:
    import nutpie  # noqa: F401
    SAMPLER = "nutpie"
except ImportError:
    SAMPLER = "pymc"


def sample(m, target_accept, seed=17):
    with m:
        return pm.sample(tune=1000, draws=1000, chains=2, target_accept=target_accept, random_seed=seed,
                         nuts_sampler=SAMPLER, progressbar=False)


def draws_of(trace, name):
    values = trace.posterior[name].values
    return values.reshape(-1, *values.shape[2:])


def interval(x, axis=0):
    return np.mean(x, axis=axis), np.quantile(x, 0.05, axis=axis), np.quantile(x, 0.95, axis=axis)



A series fit returns the curve (on the percent scale) and its linear slope per decade, over the values that have data.

def fit_series(sub, index, target_accept=0.99):
    grid = list(range(int(sub[index].min()), int(sub[index].max()) + 1))
    cells = weighted_cells(sub.assign(**{index: sub[index].astype(int)}), [index])
    trace = sample(series_model(cells, index, grid), target_accept)
    mu = draws_of(trace, "mu") * 100
    x = np.asarray(grid, float)
    observed = np.isin(x, cells[index].values)
    xs = x[observed] - x[observed].mean()
    slope = (mu[:, observed] - mu[:, observed].mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)) @ xs / (xs @ xs) * 10
    mean, lo, hi = interval(mu)
    curve = pd.DataFrame({index: grid, "mean": mean, "lo90": lo, "hi90": hi})
    return curve, dict(zip(["slope_per_decade", "slope_lo90", "slope_hi90"], map(float, interval(slope)))), trace



The period–cohort fit returns the two components and the decomposition of the total change:

the period component, standardized to the mix of birth years in the whole sample, and its linear slope per decade: the within-cohort change, the first metric in the articles;

the cohort component, at the average period;

the decomposition of the change from the first survey year to the last into generational replacement (the mix of birth years changes, period held fixed) and changing minds (the period changes, mix held fixed), averaging the two orders of the decomposition.

def fit_period_cohort(sub, target_accept=0.99):
    sub = sub.assign(cohort=sub["cohort"].astype(int))
    years = list(range(sub["year"].min(), sub["year"].max() + 1))
    cohorts = list(range(sub["cohort"].min(), sub["cohort"].max() + 1))
    cells = weighted_cells(sub, ["cohort", "year"])
    trace = sample(period_cohort_model(cells, years, cohorts), target_accept)
    alpha = draws_of(trace, "alpha")[:, None]
    cohort, period = draws_of(trace, "cohort"), draws_of(trace, "period")

    survey_years = sorted(sub["year"].unique())
    ti = {y: years.index(y) for y in survey_years}
    comp = sub.groupby(["year", "cohort"])["weight"].sum().unstack(fill_value=0).reindex(columns=cohorts, fill_value=0)
    comp = comp.div(comp.sum(axis=1), axis=0).loc[survey_years].values

    def level(mix, t):
        """Mean percent with cohort mix `mix` and the period at index t."""
        return (expit(alpha + cohort + period[:, t, None]) * mix).sum(axis=1) * 100

    y0, y1 = survey_years[0], survey_years[-1]
    p0, p1 = level(comp[0], ti[y0]), level(comp[-1], ti[y1])
    fix_cohort, fix_period = level(comp[0], ti[y1]), level(comp[-1], ti[y0])
    total = p1 - p0
    replacement = 0.5 * ((fix_period - p0) + (total - (fix_cohort - p0)))
    summary = {}
    for label, x in [("total_change", total), ("generational_replacement", replacement),
                     ("changing_minds", total - replacement)]:
        summary.update(dict(zip([label, f"{label}_lo90", f"{label}_hi90"], map(float, interval(x)))))

    pooled = sub.groupby("cohort")["weight"].sum().reindex(cohorts, fill_value=0).values
    std_period = np.stack([level(pooled / pooled.sum(), j) for j in range(len(years))], axis=1)
    x = np.array(survey_years, float) - np.mean(survey_years)
    sp = std_period[:, [ti[y] for y in survey_years]]
    slope = (sp - sp.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)) @ x / (x @ x) * 10
    summary.update(zip(["period_slope_per_decade", "period_slope_lo90", "period_slope_hi90"],
                       map(float, interval(slope))))

    mean, lo, hi = interval(std_period)
    period_df = pd.DataFrame(dict(year=years, mean=mean, lo90=lo, hi90=hi))
    mean, lo, hi = interval(expit(alpha + cohort + period.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)) * 100)
    cohort_df = pd.DataFrame(dict(cohort=cohorts, mean=mean, lo90=lo, hi90=hi))
    return period_df, cohort_df, summary, trace

The Overton paradox is about relative position: a liberal of the 1970s would be right of center today. To measure it, I estimate the distribution of latent conservatism in each group of respondents (each survey year, and each year × self-identified ideology), and express a position as a percentile of a year’s distribution.

The distributions are normal on the logit scale, estimated by weighted EM on a fine grid with the difficulties held fixed. Unlike the individual scores, they aren’t widened by measurement noise or pulled toward the prior, so their spread doesn’t depend on how many questions people answered. Positions are medians, so the percentiles are the same on any monotone scale.

XS_FINE = np.linspace(-6, 6, 121)
GROUPS = ["Liberal", "Moderate", "Conservative"]
LAST_YEAR = 2024


def latent_normals(answers, weights, d, groups, tol=1e-6, max_iter=500):
    """Mean and SD of a normal latent distribution in each group, difficulties fixed."""
    w = np.asarray(weights, dtype=float)
    labels, codes = np.unique(np.asarray(groups), return_inverse=True)
    loglike = log_likelihoods(answers, d, XS_FINE).sum(axis=0)
    like = np.exp(loglike - loglike.max(axis=1, keepdims=True))
    mu, sd = np.zeros(len(labels)), np.ones(len(labels))
    for _ in range(max_iter):
        posterior = like * norm.pdf(XS_FINE[None, :], mu[:, None], sd[:, None])[codes]
        posterior /= posterior.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
        total = np.stack([w[codes == k] @ posterior[codes == k] for k in range(len(labels))])
        m1 = total @ XS_FINE / total.sum(axis=1)
        m2 = total @ XS_FINE**2 / total.sum(axis=1)
        new_sd = np.sqrt(m2 - m1**2)
        change = max(np.abs(m1 - mu).max(), np.abs(new_sd - sd).max())
        mu, sd = m1, new_sd
        if change < tol:
            break
    return pd.DataFrame(dict(mu=mu, sd=sd), index=labels)


answers = coded.loc[keep, primary].values
dfp = df.reset_index(drop=True)
in_groups = dfp["polviews3"].isin(GROUPS).values
by_year = latent_normals(answers, dfp["weight"], d_primary.values, dfp["year"].astype(str))
by_group = latent_normals(answers[in_groups], dfp.loc[in_groups, "weight"], d_primary.values,
                          dfp.loc[in_groups, "year"].astype(str) + "|" + dfp.loc[in_groups, "polviews3"])



The reference point is the median liberal of 1974, the first year with enough self-identified liberals among the scored respondents. In each year, its percentile is the share of that year’s distribution below it.

REF_YEAR = 1974
ref = by_group.loc[f"{REF_YEAR}|Liberal", "mu"]
rows = []
for y in sorted(dfp["year"].unique()):
    dist = by_year.loc[str(y)]
    row = dict(year=y, ref_liberal=100 * norm.cdf(ref, dist["mu"], dist["sd"]))
    for g in GROUPS:
        if f"{y}|{g}" in by_group.index:
            row[g.lower()] = 100 * norm.cdf(by_group.loc[f"{y}|{g}", "mu"], dist["mu"], dist["sd"])
    rows.append(row)
position = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("year")

position[["liberal", "moderate", "conservative"]].plot(alpha=0.6, color=["C0", "C4", "C3"])
plt.plot(position.index, position["ref_liberal"], "ko-", ms=3, label=f"{REF_YEAR} liberal")
plt.axhline(50, color="0.6", lw=1)

In 2024, with 90% intervals from a bootstrap of respondents in the two years involved (the bootstrap ignores the GSS’s clustered design, so the intervals are somewhat too narrow):

def headline_numbers(sub, sub_answers):
    in_g = sub["polviews3"].isin(GROUPS).values
    year = latent_normals(sub_answers, sub["weight"], d_primary.values, sub["year"].astype(str)).loc[str(LAST_YEAR)]
    grp = latent_normals(sub_answers[in_g], sub.loc[in_g, "weight"], d_primary.values,
                         sub.loc[in_g, "year"].astype(str) + "|" + sub.loc[in_g, "polviews3"])
    out = dict(ref_liberal=100 * norm.cdf(grp.loc[f"{REF_YEAR}|Liberal", "mu"], year["mu"], year["sd"]))
    for g in GROUPS:
        out[g.lower()] = 100 * norm.cdf(grp.loc[f"{LAST_YEAR}|{g}", "mu"], year["mu"], year["sd"])
    return out


two = dfp["year"].isin([REF_YEAR, LAST_YEAR]).values
sub, sub_answers = dfp[two].reset_index(drop=True), answers[two]
point = headline_numbers(sub, sub_answers)
rng = np.random.default_rng(17)
draws = []
for _ in range(200):
    rows = np.concatenate([rng.choice(idx, len(idx)) for idx in sub.groupby("year").indices.values()])
    draws.append(headline_numbers(sub.iloc[rows].reset_index(drop=True), sub_answers[rows]))
draws = pd.DataFrame(draws)
pd.DataFrame(dict(percentile=point, lo90=draws.quantile(0.05), hi90=draws.quantile(0.95))).round(1)
